tagline.text: The seafood capital, where you feast on oysters and crab at a sunset beach

children.text: The capital of Capiz province in northern Panay, called the "Seafood Capital of the Philippines" for its fresh, cheap oysters, crab, and shrimp. In a day or two you can take in the sunset at Baybay Beach, a 19th-century cathedral and a museum in an old water tower, and Panay Church, home to one of Asia's largest church bells.

Roxas City is the capital of Capiz province, on the north coast of Panay where the Panay River meets the Sibuyan Sea. A mid-sized city of about 180,000 people, it has become one of the Philippines' foremost seafood-producing areas, thanks to its wide river mouth, shallow seas, and fish farms scattered throughout the area. Locals call it the "Seafood Capital of the Philippines," and oysters, crab, shrimp, and shellfish often cost half what they do in Manila.
The city's history began in
, when a Spanish expedition established a settlement here. It was originally named Capis, the same as the province, and when it became a city in

, it took its current name in honor of Manuel Roxas, a native son who became the first president of the Third Philippine Republic. A statue of President Roxas and a historical marker stand in the plaza in front of city hall, and the old town — where the bridge over the Panay River, the provincial capitol, and the cathedral all cluster together — is easy to explore on foot.

The name Capiz is also well known for capiz shell, the translucent shell once used in place of window glass. These shells once lit up the windows of Spanish-era Philippine mansions, and are still crafted into lampshades, wind chimes, and ornaments as souvenirs today. Just outside the city is Santa Monica Church in Panay, home to one of Asia's largest church bells, so you can combine great food with a walk through small-town history.

This suits travelers who want the relaxed feel of a provincial city and hearty seafood over flashy attractions, or those touring around Panay Island between Boracay and Iloilo. The beach has gray sand, so it's better thought of as a place for walking, watching the sunset, and eating seafood rather than swimming.

blocks.title: Sunset and seafood at Baybay Beach

children.text: About
3km

from downtown, Baybay Beach is lined with restaurants and paluto stalls, where you pick your seafood and have it cooked to order. Watching the sun set over the Sibuyan Sea while eating oysters and crab is the heart of a Roxas trip.

A public park called "La Playa de Roxas," built along Baybay Beach. With a beachfront promenade and a seafood center together, it fills with local families in the evening. Along the shore, traces of an old stone watchtower built to guard against Spanish-era pirates also remain.
The cathedral across from the city hall plaza, completed in
. Its cream-colored facade, bell tower, and front-yard fountain together give the old town its face.
A cylindrical water tower built in
to store water for the dry season, converted into a museum in
. Old photographs of Capiz, everyday artifacts, and traditional crafts can be viewed for free.
The bell tower of Santa Monica Church in Panay, about
15–20 minutes
east of downtown by car, holds a massive bell weighing about 10 tons, cast in
. The church itself, built with thick coral-stone walls, is a sight worth seeing on its own.

Lampshades, wind chimes, and picture frames made from the translucent, glowing capiz shell are the region's signature souvenirs. You can choose from various sizes at souvenir shops and the market downtown.
A small island off Roxas, about
30–45 minutes
by bangka from Culasi wharf. You can enjoy a fishing village and snorkeling in clear water — only go on days when the sea is calm.

blocks.title: Walking the Panay riverside and old town

children.text: Roxas City Bridge, the provincial capitol, city hall, and the President Roxas statue all cluster along the riverside. Walking the riverside in the cool of morning or evening lets you see the everyday life of a simple provincial city up close.

Culasi Port, north of Roxas City, has at times had passenger ferries running to and from Manila, but the routes and schedules change often. If traveling by boat, check the shipping line's notices first; generally, flying or going overland via Iloilo is more convenient.
Travel between downtown and Baybay Beach is by tricycle or jeepney. A shared tricycle costs about
per person, and a chartered one about
Panay can be reached by jeepney from downtown, and a half-day chartered tricycle (about

is the wet season with frequent showers, and when a typhoon crosses northern Panay, flights can be cancelled and areas around the Panay River can flood.
The city's signature festival is "Sinadya sa Halaran," held in the
first week of December
, timed to the Immaculate Conception feast day on
December 8
, the city's patron saint. Street parades, a river boat procession, and food markets fill the city with a festive mood. Lodging downtown fills up quickly during this period, so book ahead.

In Roxas, seafood is non-negotiable. Plump oysters (talaba) are eaten raw, grilled, or grilled with cheese on top, while crab and shrimp are sautéed in garlic butter or coconut milk. At the seafood center on Baybay Beach, the standard practice is paluto: you pick your seafood by weight from a tank or ice display, choose how it's cooked, and it's prepared on the spot. Angel wing clams (diwal) are subject to harvest restrictions at times to protect the resource, so they aren't always available. Popular gifts include processed seafood like dried squid, dried fish, and shrimp paste.
Many paluto places charge separately for the seafood by weight and for the cooking fee. Be sure to confirm the price per kilogram and the cooking fee before ordering.
The sunset at Baybay Beach is usually most beautiful around
. Arrive a bit early to grab a spot on the beach.
The beach has gray sand and the water is often shallow and murky. For swimming in clear water, it's better to go to Olotayan Island or Islas de Gigantes.
To see the Panay Church Bell up close, you need to climb the bell tower stairs. Ask the parish office whether it's open, and view it quietly during Mass times.
Planning a trip across Panay by bus, linking Boracay–Roxas–Iloilo, lets you see three cities with just one flight.
Downtown has ATMs and shopping malls, but seafood stalls and tricycles are cash-only.
Seafood restaurants get crowded during the December festival and holidays, so eat dinner a bit earlier.
Raw oysters and clams carry a food poisoning risk during periods of high water temperature. Avoid shellfish when a red tide (harmful algal bloom) warning is in effect, and check local notices.
For island trips like Olotayan, choose a boat with life jackets, and postpone if winds are strong.
During the wet season and typhoon period, areas around the Panay River and low-lying areas can flood, so check weather advisories.
Seafood without a listed price can end up costing more than expected at checkout, so ask for the total before ordering.
Inside churches, cover your shoulders and knees, and avoid taking photos during Mass.
Avoid walking alone along the beach late at night, and keep a close eye on your belongings.
